title: I shipped a top-down tactical stealth game in Godot in about a month, with an AI coding assistant doing most of the programming. Here’s how the split worked
author: dystostorm
selftext:
Silent Entry is out on itch.io (Windows/Linux): a top-down tactical stealth game where you lead a police team through ten hostage missions. https://dystostorm.itch.io/silent-entry



How it was made



Me: the design and direction, playtesting, every judgment call on feel, the music (composed in Cubase), and the final say on everything.

The AI (Claude, through Claude Code): most of the code (\~26,000 lines of GDScript) and the tools around it.

What worked



Tests as the safety net. 152 scripted gameplay scenarios (breach a door, talk a suspect down, snipe through a window) run headless after every change. The AI writes a scenario for every new mechanic.

Art as code instead of AI images. The 3D world is built procedurally from the 2D level maps. Characters come from scripted Blender files, and animations are Mixamo. No image generators.

It checks its own work visually. It takes screenshots of the game and reviews them before showing me anything.

Even the trailer footage is rendered by the game itself from scripted “shots”, then encoded with ffmpeg.

What didn’t



Tests only catch what they test. Two bugs shipped in the tutorial because the tests ran in conditions real players never hit: the lock station broke when a new game rolled a random door layout. My playtesting found them, not the AI.

You still have to play it constantly. “The test passes” and “it feels right” are different things.

Happy to answer questions about the workflow.
